In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis and evaluation of new agents for the treatment of cancer.
the synthesis of natural products, the design and synthesis of analogs and the evaluation of these agents for their ability to induce cell cycle arrest in cancer cells.
the development of novel chemical approaches for the preparation of new natural products with potential as anti-cancer agents and their subsequent biological evaluation.

we have been very lucky.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemistry and biology associated with tubulin polymerizing natural products has been extremely rewarding, and we look forward to continuing this work in the years to come.
the epothilone A is the most potent tubulin polymerizing agent yet discovered, with activity against the multidrug resistant P-glycoprotein.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the taxanes, epothilones and sarcodictyin are all highly active against a variety of cancer cells and are also active against multidrug resistant cells.
the taxanes, epothilones and eleutherobins have a common mechanism of action.
the tubulin polymerization mechanism of taxol is a highly selective process and the design of analogs with improved activity and/or reduced toxicity is not a trivial matter.
